title: Dorton v. Collins & Aikman Corp.
summary: An acceptance is “expressly conditional” under § 2-207(1) only if it clearly tells the offeror that the offeree will not proceed without assent to its additional terms; a form saying the sale was “subject to” its printed conditions did not qualify, so whether the arbitration clause entered the carpet contracts depended on § 2-207(2) and findings the district court had not made.

sections.Parties: Frank E. Dorton and his partners, doing business as The Carpet Mart in Kingsport, Tennessee, were the plaintiffs and appellees; they bought carpet for resale and claimed the seller misrepresented its fiber content. Collins & Aikman Corporation, a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in New York and a carpet plant in Dalton, Georgia, was the defendant and appellant seeking to enforce arbitration language in its printed sales forms. Both were merchants.
sections.Material Facts: From 1968 through 1970 the parties did more than fifty-five carpet transactions. Orders were telephoned to Collins & Aikman’s Georgia order department, sometimes by a Carpet Mart partner and sometimes through the seller’s visiting salesman; the parties disputed whether those calls themselves produced oral agreements. After checking price and credit the seller mailed a printed acknowledgment, in several versions, whose face said the transaction was subject to the terms on both sides and purported to bind the buyer by signing, giving shipping directions, accepting delivery, or in some versions keeping the form ten days without objection; the reverse required arbitration in New York City of disputes connected with the contract. The acknowledgment usually arrived before the carpet. The Carpet Mart accepted delivery and paid without objecting. In May 1970 a customer complaint led it to discover that carpet supposedly made entirely of Kodel polyester allegedly contained a cheaper, inferior fiber.
sections.Procedural History: The Carpet Mart sued in Tennessee state court for fraud, deceit and misrepresentation, seeking $450,000 in compensatory and punitive damages. Collins & Aikman removed the case on diversity grounds and moved under § 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act to stay the litigation pending arbitration. The district court found no binding arbitration agreement: it applied § 2-207(3), treated the transactions as contracts formed by conduct, and excluded the seller’s unmatched arbitration clause. The seller appealed the denial of the stay, appealable under 28 U.S.C. § 1292. The Sixth Circuit, Judge Celebrezze writing, remanded on January 6, 1972 for findings on whether the oral dealings formed contracts, whether arbitration was already part of them, and if not whether it materially altered them; Judge Brooks participated but died before the opinion was filed.
sections.Issue: Did the seller’s acknowledgments make acceptance expressly conditional on the buyer’s assent to additional terms, so that the writings formed no contract and § 2-207(3) governed? If instead they were acceptances or confirmations under § 2-207(1), did the arbitration clause enter the contracts under subsection (2)? If it did, could the buyer’s fraud claims proceed in court without a stay?
sections.Holding: An acceptance is expressly conditional within § 2-207(1) only when it clearly conveys that the offeree will not proceed without the offeror’s assent to the additional or different terms. The seller’s “subject to” language and its provisions treating various acts or silence as acceptance did not meet that standard, so the district court could not bypass subsections (1) and (2) by applying subsection (3). If arbitration was additional to the oral offers or agreements, it had to be evaluated under subsection (2), where, between merchants, material alteration was the central question requiring factual findings; the court did not decide whether this clause was material. If the clause was part of the contracts, its breadth reached the fraud claims and required a stay. Remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Section 2-207 answers the commercial practice of exchanging forms whose boilerplate never matches. Under the mirror-image rule a response adding terms became a counteroffer; the Code lets a contract exist despite differing boilerplate and decides separately which added terms enter, so treating every qualified acknowledgment as a counteroffer would undo the statutory design. Two factual questions came first: whether the telephone dealings already completed contracts, making the acknowledgments confirmations rather than acceptances, and whether arbitration was in fact new. The conditional-acceptance proviso demanded more than a declaration that the seller’s terms governed: it required an express condition tied to the buyer’s assent, and a form offering several ways to bind the buyer did not distinctly say the seller would refuse to proceed without assurance of assent. Once the acknowledgments were acceptances or confirmations, subsection (2) governed the added clause; the court left materiality to the trial court. Finally, under Prima Paint a broad arbitration clause, if agreed, covers a claim that the sale was induced by fraud, because the buyer attacked the carpet rather than the procurement of the clause itself.

priorVersions.summary: “Subject to” the seller’s terms did not clearly make acceptance conditional on the buyer’s assent; arbitration’s inclusion required further findings.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Sixth Circuit (1972).

Important remand questions: Was there an oral contract? Was arbitration already a term? If newly proposed, did it materially alter the bargain? Compare C. Itoh’s explicitly conditional language and Bayway’s discussion of a different jurisdiction’s arbitration rule.

sections.Parties: The Carpet Mart partners sued Collins & Aikman, their carpet supplier, for alleged fraud and misrepresentation about fiber quality.
sections.Material Facts: The parties made about fifty-five transactions over three years. The buyer ordered by telephone; the seller sent acknowledgments containing arbitration on the reverse. The forms used “subject to” language and purported to make retaining the form or accepting delivery sufficient. The buyer received and paid for carpets without objecting.
sections.Procedural History: After removal on diversity grounds, the district court denied a stay pending arbitration, using § 2-207(3) to exclude the clause. The Sixth Circuit remanded for further factual findings under the correct formation and term-selection analysis.
sections.Issue: Did the forms prevent formation under § 2-207(1), and, if not, was arbitration already agreed or added through § 2-207(2)?
sections.Holding: The forms did not clearly condition acceptance on the buyer’s assent in the statutory sense. Whether arbitration became a term required findings about the prior oral transactions and material alteration.
sections.Reasoning: The proviso requires a clear indication that the offeree will not proceed without assurance of assent to the additional or different terms. “Subject to” and a list of conduct or inaction purportedly sufficient to bind the buyer did not meet that standard. An acknowledgment could be an acceptance or a confirmation of an already completed oral contract. Arbitration might even have been part of the oral bargain. If it was an additional term, both parties’ merchant status brought § 2-207(2) into play, and materiality required facts. The opinion does not categorically hold all arbitration clauses immaterial or all material.

learning.why: Dorton is the first fork in the § 2-207 analysis. Its result depends on the precise conditional language and on distinguishing a new acceptance from confirmation of an earlier oral agreement.

topics.battle-forms: Formation and term inclusion require separate statutory steps.
topics.conditional-acceptance: The court demands a clear unwillingness to proceed without assent.
topics.additional-terms: An added arbitration provision must be assessed under subsection (2).
topics.material-alteration: Materiality remained a factual issue for remand.
topics.arbitration: The dispute concerned whether an agreement to arbitrate had entered the contracts.
topics.assent: Silence and performance do not automatically establish assent to every printed term.
